M3L11. Negotiation Biases 
 
Slide #1
 
In this topic, we will discuss the major judgment biases in negotiation. 
 
Slide #2
 
We are going to discuss some specific judgment biases that we are subject to when 
negotiating with others. 
 
 
 
Slide #3
 
When negotiators at both sides assume their interests are in direct conflict, they will 
begin the negotiation with a win-lose competitive attitude. 
This kind of bias occurs to less experienced negotiators or in negotiations with a 
tight schedule.  
Both parties spend insufficient time identifying opportunities to create actual value. 
Slide #4
 
Another unique psychological behavior that negotiators exhibit is that negotiators 
tend to be attached to their proposal in the negotiation. 
The negotiator's “I win you lose” attitude drives them to focus on convincing their 
counterparts to accept their proposals rather than asking questions to identify value 
adding opportunities. 
Slide #5
 
Framing your proposal in a positive or negative way makes a huge difference in 
negotiation. 
 
 
 
Slide #6
 
For example, your department proposed 500,000 dollars for an engineering 
consulting project. 
The total cost is 400,000 dollars including overhead. When you presented the 
proposal to your client, they pushed back and would like to pay 450,000 dollars.  
Does this counteroffer represent a 50,000 dollar loss or a 50,000 dollar gain in 
comparison with your current target? 
Slide #7
 
People with positive frames are more likely to make an agreement, so it is important 
to lead the opposition toward a positive frame when presenting a proposal. 
Always show them the positive perspective of your proposal. 
 
Slide #8
 
Now, let's discuss the escalation of conflict in negotiation and how to solve it.  
One of the golden rules of negotiation is to match your counterpart's strategy.  
Because of this, when one party initiates a conflict, the other party is likely to follow 
with the same course of action. 
Then each party is focused almost exclusively on beating the other side.  
They are primed to escalate their commitment to their initial course of action. Here 
are some classic examples about escalation of conflict. 
Slide #9
 
The first example is the 1994 and 1995 Major League Baseball strike.  
The owners of baseball teams, baseball players, and the league could not reach an 
agreement on the payment to the baseball players. 
Their conflict escalated pretty fast by the end of the baseball player’s strike.  
Owners lost 375 million dollars in 1994 and 326 million dollars in 1995.  
Players also lost money, status, and bargaining power.  
It took the league and the players several years to recover from this catastrophic 
incident. 
Slide #10
 
Four years later, basketball players and the NBA league fell into this escalation of 
conflict trap again. 
Basketball players and the league escalated their conflict over the player's salary. The 
basketball players refused and the league lost 1 billion dollars.  
Players lost 500 million dollars.  
The consequence of escalation of conflict in negotiation is catastrophic.  
It always leads to both parties walking away from the negotiation. 
 
Slide #11
 
How to solve escalation of conflict when it occurs in a negotiation.  
Once we become aware of the possible reason or the basis for a conflict, we can take 
steps to mitigate defensive behavior to find solutions.  
To do so, we must first recognize that cooperation is the key.  
We must understand that we cannot impose our own resolution on someone who is 
in a defensive pose. 
The other person must be part of the solution by being included.  
Through a cooperative effort, both parties can find a mutual resolution.  
If both parties do not trust each other, then cooperation is impossible.  
Both parties need to identify negotiators that both can trust.  
If they cannot find someone within their own organizations, they may use a mediator 
to help rebuild mutual trust. 
 
Slide #12
 
We've learned that people, including negotiators, tend to overvalue their 
possessions.  
Negotiators tend to overestimate not only the value of his offer, but also the chance 
that the offer would be accepted by the other party.  
But in reality, conventional wisdom says that something is worth whatever a buyer is 
willing to pay for it. 
 
Slide #13
 
How to manage this endowment bias?  
The first is to gain more knowledge about our object.  
We can become knowledgeable by collecting additional market intelligence and 
analyzing similar business cases.  
The second way is to seek objective value assessment from a neutral party.  
If feasible, we can even hire a consultant to help us conduct an objective due 
diligence about the object. 
The more knowledge we have, the more objective we become about the value of 
what we own. 
Slide #14
 
Let us now discuss self-serving bias in negotiation and how to overcome it.  
In a negotiation situation, a negotiator exhibits self-serving bias, means that person 
focuses on his own position and not giving enough attention to his counterpart's 
interest. 
I want to point out the self-serving bias describes an individual's behavior when 
interacting with others in a negotiation situation.  
It is different from individual cognitive bias that we learned in previous lectures, 
which describes an individual's psychological behavior when making his own 
judgment calls. 
 
Slide #15
 
For example, my accounting department asked my team to help them negotiate a 
settlement with a company which declined to pay a licensing fee.  
I had a member named Tom to handle this case.  
My accounting colleagues unintentionally planted the self-serving bias in Tom's 
mind.  
The company failed to fulfill its contract obligations. 
So, Tom prepared his negotiation with this kind of a self-serving attitude.  
At the beginning of negotiation with the company, Tom presented a position letter 
with detailed information to explain the amount of fees that the company owes us.  
The company immediately argued that the claim was unfair and not right. 
 
Slide #16
 
So, the first step to realize the self-serving bias is to be aware that your initial 
judgment on your counterpart may not be correct.  
Try to be objective and very beginning.  
Your attitude is everything.  
Try to understand the other side's problems and interest before judging them. 
Explore underlying interests of other parties’ positions and actions. 
 
Slide #17
 
The second practice is focus on your desired goal rather than your judgment.  
Term-sheet and analytical assessment plays a large role in helping you focus on the 
desired outcome.  
Please use the term-sheet. 
 
 
Slide #18
 
React constructively to different opinions, critics, and rejections.  
Separate people from problems. 
Be willing to solve problems together with your counterpart. 
 
 
Slide #19
 
One of the most frequently asked questions about negotiation is about who should 
make the first offer.  
The rule is never make the first offer before you understand your needs and your 
partner's needs and interests.  
However, you can make the first offer if you have sufficient information about the 
market and you are more knowledgeable about the market than your counterpart. 
 
Slide #20
 
When your counterpart anchors an offer and you do not like it, you should 
immediately reject the offer before making your counteroffer.  
It is hard to do it in a constructive way and my suggestion can be.  
I am not playing a game with you, but your offer is too far away from my acceptable

Then make your counterpart offer with justification. 
Remember, always give a justification for your counteroffer.

The second approach is to ignore the offer.  
I always use this kind of statement.

M3L2. Excessive Competition

Slide #2
 
The escalation of disruptive competition is common in the business world.  
There are many examples of escalated competition that are unsound.  
Even the big players can be drawn into this kind of irrational escalation. 
 
 
Slide #3

that can be had from this type of programs.  
Back in 1981, American Airlines introduced the first frequent flyer program. It was 
truly a unique marketing plan. Anyone who flew regularly could redeem their travel 
miles for rewards. Brilliant idea!  
Taking American Airlines lead, all the other competitors jumped on the bandwagon

industry when oil companies found out winners of oil field auctions always ended up 
losing money from their bids. 
There was no accurate method to estimate the potential value of an offshore oil field 
at that time. So as the intrinsic value of an oil field is not clear cut, oil companies 
might guess its value to be anywhere within a range, say between 50 million dollars 
to 100 million dollars.  
The company who made the highest estimation and placed a bid at that level would 
win the auction. 
Later, the company found that it was not worth that much. 
 
Slide #3
 
Some factors contribute to the winner's curse.  
Companies may have access to different information and also companies may 
interpret the same information in a different way.  
The third factor is a psychological factor. Companies may make different decisions 
based on their beliefs and based on how they look at the problem. 
The desire to win or avoid certain loss leads to risk seeking behavior in a competitive 
bidding process.  
So, people tend to be irrational and push prices beyond the true value of the asset 
involved. 
Slide #4
 
One recent example is the intense bidding war between AT&T and Verizon Wireless 
in 2017 over the acquisition of a company called Straight Path Communications. 
Straight Path Communications is an entity spun out from IDT Corporation in 2013, 
primarily to hold wireless spectrum assets in the 28 through 39 gigahertz bands, 
which are the spectrum for fifth generation communication. Straight Path 
Communications, which had just nine employees in October 2016 was worth about 
$400 million because of the wireless spectrum it held. 
Slide #5
 
As the 4G wireless communication competition heated up in 2016, Verizon Wireless 
and AT&T suffered significant loss from a wireless subscriber perspective.  
Verizon reported a loss of over 300,000 wireless subscribers in the fourth quarter of 
2016 and AT&T lost 256,000.  
Both companies wanted to strategically position themselves to compete on the next 
generation service, 5G wireless communication, in the future by acquiring high 
frequency wireless spectrum assets. 
 
Slide #6
 
AT&T started a war with a preemptive approach. It offered 1.6 billion dollars to take 
over straight path communications. In April, 2017, the price was more than three 
times of straight Path communications book value.  
At that time, a month later, Verizon joined the war and offered $3.1 billion or $184 
per share, which was twice of what 80 and t offered and won the bidding war. 
 
Slide #7
 
The rapid escalation of the bidding war between AT&T and Verizon surprised many 
investors in the communication industry. Both AT&T and Verizon appeared to 
materially overestimate the value of the Spectrum asset that Straight Path 
Communications owned. In particular, Verizon's response to AT&T's bid seemed a bit 
aimless as it seemed to have had a fear of missing out on these licenses after AT&T'S 
initial bid, the telecommunication industry was unclear on what the 5G network 
would look like in the end. 
Both companies appear to be irrationally racing to gather assets presumed to be 
useful in the future. It is still too early to tell whether Verizon will earn a reasonable 
return from its 3.1 billion dollar investment in the asset. But one fact is obvious, AT&T 
and other carriers did not believe that straight path communication spectrum was 
worth Verizon paid. 
M3L4. Game Theory 
 
Slide #1
 
In this topic, we will describe game theory and how to avoid excessive competition. 
Slide #2
 
One way to avoid falling into the competitive escalation of commitment is to be 
rational and cooperative in a competitive environment.  
Markets are both competitive and cooperative. Companies earn higher payoffs when 
they select the constructive course of action in a competitive environment. 
Game theory is an advanced strategic model for cooperative companies to compete 
in a constructive manner to create value for a whole industry for all the players that 
participate in the competition.  
Game theory is widely accepted by the strategists in the industry. 
Slide #3
 
Here is an example.  
Consider two technology giants who are deciding between introducing a radical new 
alloy material for oil wells that could earn them hundreds of millions of dollars in 
profit or introducing an improved version of an older technology that would earn 
them much less. 
 
Slide #4
 
If both companies decide to introduce the new technology, the market will accept 
the technology better.  
And they would each earn 600 million dollars. But if only one company wants to 
introduce the new technology to the market, the market adoption will be worse. 
And also the company needs to absorb all development costs of the new technology. 
So the company who introduced the technology would only earn 150 million dollars. 
The other company who does not want to introduce the technology, would lose 
market share and earn nothing.  
Another scenario is both companies decide not to introduce new technologies. 
They will continue splitting the existing market and each earn 300 million dollars 
from the existing market. 
 
Slide #5
 
Another application of game theory in the oil industry is the technology and 
engineering consortium that major oil firms sponsor.  
The consortium develops new technologies, share risk, and grow new market out of 
the new technologies.  
At the same time, each company develops its own version of product of the 
technology and gain competitive advantage over each other to split the market that 
they created together. 
M3L5. Decision-Making in Negotiation 
 
Slide #1
 
Now, let us switch gears to discuss decision-making in negotiation. 
 
Slide #2
 
Negotiation requires instant decisions based on limited information. Sophisticated 
negotiators carefully exchange information to influence counterparts, to make 
judgment calls that mutually benefit both parties.  
As an engineering manager, you are negotiating with a lot of people on different 
topics every day. For instance, you negotiate the specifications of a new product with 
your peer engineers. You may negotiate an order contract with an important client or 
with suppliers.  
Negotiation in the real world is very different from what is shown in the movies.  
In the real world, business negotiation takes a lot of preparation and analysis. 
Negotiators make rational decisions in negotiations. 
Slide #3
 
The analytical structure of business negotiation starts with the assessment of three 
key sets of information. 
 
 
 
Slide #4
 
The first is to identify the business terms or topics that each party wants to include in 
the agreement. These terms are not equally important to different parties. 
So you also need to determine what terms are non-negotiable that you absolutely 
require. These terms are so important to your company that they prevent you from 
entering into an agreement with your counterpart if you cannot get an agreement on 
those terms.  
You also need to make a list of terms on which you are willing to compromise or 
negotiate. 
In addition, you need to identify the terms that are unimportant for you, and you 
want to explore how important they are to your counterpart. 
Slide #5
 
Business negotiation is a two-way process.  
It is important to understand your counterpart's interests.  
What terms your partner wants to include in the agreement and their relative 
importance to your counterpart? 
 
 
Slide #6
 
The third set of critical information is your and your counterpart's bottom line.  
The power of negotiation comes from each party's best alternative to a negotiated 
agreement or BATNA.  
BATNA is the key focus and the driving force behind a successful negotiation.  
The BATNA is often seen by negotiators not as a safety net but rather as a point of 
leverage in negotiations. 
Many managers invest too little time in researching their real options and 
misestimate their BATNA.  
This can lead to poor or faulty decision making and negotiating result.  
Negotiators also need to be aware of other negotiators’ BATNA and to identify how 
it compares to what they are offering. 
Slide #7
 
In negotiation, the best alternative to a negotiated agreement or BATNA is the best 
alternative course of action a partner can take if negotiations fail and an agreement 
cannot be reached. 
A party should generally not accept a worse solution than its BATNA.  
Care should be taken to ensure that deals are equitably valued, considering all 
considerations, such as relationship value, time value of money, or the possibility that 
your plan B may work.  
Those other considerations are often difficult to value, since they are generally based 
on uncertain or qualitative considerations, rather than easily measurable and 
quantifiable factors. 
 
Slide #8
 
Start searching early, as it usually takes more time than most expect to develop their 
BATNA to the stage where it becomes actionable during negotiation.  
If you start too late, you may not come up with a valid BATNA when you need it.  
Another thing we need to pay attention to is do not focus exclusively on your 
BATNA. 
We need to give enough thought or research into uncovering our counterpart’s 
BATNA, their bottom lines, so that we know how far we can push, how hard we can 
push. 
M3L6. Two Types of Negotiation 
 
Slide #1
 
In this topic, we continue the explanation of negotiation and introduce the two types 
of negotiation. 
Slide #2
 
Whenever we are trying to reach a goal and need help of another party who has 
different preferences, we negotiate.  
In most negotiations, we face two goals, claiming value and creating value.  
Value can be defined as anything you would like to get out of a negotiation, whether 
it will be more dollars, a consulting contract, an end to conflict, and so on. 
There are two typical ways to negotiate. 
Slide #3
 
The first approach is called distributive negotiation or win-lose approach.  
This is also called competitive zero-sum or claiming value approach.  
This approach is based on the assumption that one person can win only at the 
expense of the other. It has the following three characteristics. 
First, there are fixed resources to be divided, so that the more one gets, the less the 
other gets. That is why this is called a zero-sum approach.  
The second characteristic is one person's interest opposes the other's. There is no 
synergy between the interests of both parties.  
The dominant concern in this type of bargaining is usually to maximize one's own 
interest. 
One side wins and the other side loses. 
Slide #4
 
The basic tactics open to negotiators in this kind of a distributive approach are to 
learn as much as possible about the other person's position, especially regarding 
resistance point, and influence the other person to believe what is possible.  
At the same time, negotiators need to carefully protect their information, not to let 
their counterparts know their motivations, their interests. 
 
Slide #5
 
The second approach is a more constructive approach. It is called integrative 
negotiation or win-win approach.  
This negotiation approach is also called collaborative or creating value approach. It is 
superior to all negotiation approaches. It results in both the parties feeling that they 
are achieving what they want. It results in satisfaction to both parties.  
This approach is also called creating value because the goal here is how both sides 
leave the negotiation table feeling they have created value together out of their 
collective interests. 
Slide #6
 
The win-win approach is suitable for situations with the following characteristics. 
First, there is synergy between both parties, and both parties are willing to create 
actual value out of the synergy.  
The second is, there are sufficient resources to be divided, and both sides can win. 
Because of that, the dominating concern in the win-win approach is to maximize joint 
outcomes. 
Slide #7
 
The primary strategies for the win-win approach include cooperation, sharing 
information, and mutual problem solving. 
M3L7. Distributive Negotiation 
 
Slide #1
 
In this topic, we will discuss the distributive type of negotiation. 
 
Slide #2
 
At times, a negotiation will only have a distributive component. That is, there is only 
opportunity to claim value and not to create value. You might have difficulty finding 
other issues to add to the mix when negotiating the price for a new car. 
 
 
Slide #3
 
Distributive negotiations always follow a bargaining process. 
 A buyer or seller makes the first offer.  
The buyer's first offer should be lower than his highest accepted price or resistance 
point or BATNA.  
The seller's first offer should be higher than his resistance point.  
After some rounds of bargaining, they reach an agreement that falls between the 
buyer's and seller's resistance points in the shadow field of the value claiming chart. 
The shadow zone is also called zone of possible agreement or ZOPA. 
 
Slide #4
 
Although the distributive approach is not the most desirable negotiation approach, 
there are still several things we can do to improve our negotiation skills and prepare 
to claim more value from this win-and-lose situation. 
 
 
Slide #5
 
The first thing we can do is to assess and improve our BATNA.  
In negotiation, our best alternative to a negotiated agreement, or BATNA, is often 
our strongest source of power. 
When we have a strong alternative, we will be ready to walk away from any deal that 
is inferior to our BATNA.  
Wise negotiators not only assess their BATNA before negotiating, but also spend 
considerable time working to try to improve it.  
For example, buyer may continue to search for other sellers while negotiating a 
particular offer or may try to negotiate one or more offers at the same time. 
 
Slide #6
 
The second is to calculate your resistance point or reservation point.  
In distributive negotiation, your resistance point is typically your BATNA.  
You always have one alternative, which is no deal.  
Because your resistance point is your bottom line, it is the least amount you are 
willing to accept.  
It is generally wise not to share it with your counterpart across the table, even if you 
trust and like the other party. 
Because they will take advantage of your BATNA and claim more value from the 
zero-sum negotiation. 
Slide #7
 
It is important not only to determine your own BATNA and reservation point, but 
also to estimate your counterpart's BATNA and their reservation point.  
This knowledge will help you determine how far you can push the other side. 
We can make these estimates by thinking about and researching the other party's 
alternatives and resources, such as how much they might have to spend and what 
other negotiating opportunities may arise for them. 
Slide #8
 
The fourth step is to evaluate the ZOPA, the zone of possible agreement.  
When you have a sense of each party's reservation point, you will be able to evaluate 
the ZOPA. 
The ZOPA includes the range of all possible deals that both parties will find 
acceptable.  
A thoughtful assessment of both parties ZOPA will help you claim more value from 
the acceptable range. 
M3L8. Integrative Negotiation 
 
Slide #1
 
In this topic, we will discuss integrative negotiation. 
 
Slide #2
 
The win-win approach is most desirable for business negotiation in that the 
collaborative process creates value for both parties.  
We have discussed the strategy to claim value in a distributive negotiation situation. 
Far more often, however, there are hidden sources of value you can add to the 
discussion to create value. 
Here is an example of integrative negotiation. 
Slide #3
 
A biotech company A owns a long-term contract for pharmaceutical grade egg 
supply. The company uses the eggs to make protein products as raw materials for 
the food and pharmaceutical industries.  
Another biotech company B also uses eggs to make antibiotics. 
In 2008, the market faced a significant egg shortage due to the breakout of chicken 
flu across the world. 
Slide #4
 
So company B wanted to purchase some eggs from biotech company A.  
Company B needed at least $100 million worth of A, but company A could only 
provide half of that.  
There is no overlap between their resistance points or Zopa. 
After several runs of unproductive negotiations, the negotiators from the two 
companies realized there is no middle point for them to reach an agreement.  
However, when the two companies talked about their interest in the eggs and their 
operations, they eventually realized that Company A only needed the egg white to 
make protein while Company B only needed egg yolk to make the antibiotics. 
Also, Company B owned a state-of-the-art egg separation facility in California, which 
has extra capacity that Company A may use to process their eggs.  
The two companies identified a hidden synergy between them and created actual 
value for both parties.  
Company A will use Company B's egg separation facility to separate egg white and 
yolk. 
Company B would keep the egg yolk to make antibiotics and Company A will get the 
processed egg white to make proteins.  
The outcome of the win-win negotiation is that Company A reduced its egg 
processing cost and received extra income from the excess eggs that it sold to 
Company B.  
At the same time, Company B had a sustainable supply of egg yolk and fulfilled the 
unused capacity of its egg processing plant. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Slide #5
 
Some of the guidelines to the integrative approach are: 
 
 
 
 
Slide #6
 
First, orient yourself toward a win-win approach.  
Your attitude while going into negotiation plays a huge role in the outcome.  
To build trust with the other party, I suggest using constructive wording rather than 
destructive wording during the negotiation. 
For example, I use discussion rather than negotiation in my communication with my 
counterpart to emphasize my desired collaborative approach. 
Slide #7
 
The second is to have a concrete strategy and apply your discussion accordingly. 
Collaborative negotiation requires information sharing and mutual problem solving. 
We want to give each part enough time to share the information, ask questions, and 
solve the problems together. 
Slide #8
 
The third is to be clear on what is important to you and why it is important.  
This involves internal discussions with different units of your company to understand 
how these terms create value for your company as a whole. 
Also, it is important to develop your best alternative to a negotiated agreement or 
BATNA. 
Slide #9
 
When you discuss the terms with your counterpart, focus on interest, not positions.  
Consider the other party's situation.  
Ask questions, use active listening skills, rephrase, and ask questions again.  
We need to pay a lot of attention to the flow of negotiation. 
 
Slide #10
 
Another good practice is to create options for mutual gain. and generate a variety of 
possibilities before deciding what to do.  
One practice I always use to test my counterpart's interests is to provide multiple 
options that are equally important to me and ask my counterpart which one gives 
them more value. 
By asking follow up questions, we can figure out each other's interests and potential 
synergies. 
Slide #11
 
One guidance is to take the intangible into account.  
Communicate carefully, especially when we negotiate with international parties. We 
must pay extra attention to the cultural difference.  
Companies in different cultures may be more sensitive to some specific business 
issues. 
For example, Asian companies are very strategic and appreciate personal relationship 
when doing business with each other.  
They feel comfortable to share information with their partners only after they build 
mutual trust with each other. 
M3L9a. Systematic Negotiation Process 
 
Slide #1
 
In this topic, we will discuss the systematic negotiation process. 
 
Slide #2
 
A systematic negotiation process includes four major steps.  
The first step is collecting business information to prepare for the negotiation.  
The second step is to analyze the information to calculate business positions of 
different offer options. 
After that, we will engage our partners to exchange information and understand each 
other's business interests.  
The fourth step is to make business judgment about the information that we will 
learn from our discussions with our partners.  
It is not uncommon that we repeat the process several times to fully understand each 
other's business needs, limitations, and offers to reach final agreement. 
The information collection and the business analysis require structured rational 
assessment, while the engagement and judgment steps rely on managers intuitive 
reasoning. 
Slide #3
 
We can use a term-sheet as a framework to help us identify terms to negotiate, as 
well as collect business information. 
 
 
 
Slide #4
 
Here is an example of a term-sheet that we will use in technology license 
negotiation. 
A term-sheet should include at least the following information.  
The first is negotiation terms or issues which are listed in the first column of this 
table. For example, the license technology, royalty, and so on. Other issues we want 
to negotiate.  
The second set of information to collect is about the relative importance of each 
term to our organization. Such type of information includes company strategy 
statement, business performance objectives, key performance indicators, research 
and development capabilities, and so on. These terms are rarely equally important to 
our company, and we need to weigh them differently when trading issues in the 
negotiation. 
Also, we can mark what items are negotiable and what are non-negotiable. Do not 
forget listing those items that are not important to you, but likely important to your 
partners. Those items are your source of leverage. 
Slide #5
 
The third set of information we need to collect is the market information about the 
product and potential partners, so that we can determine the fair market value of 
each item. 
Each issue should include three position points. 
 
Slide #6
 
One is the desired outcome, which represents our wish under best-case scenario. 
 
 
 
Slide #7
 
The second point is the expected outcome, which represents the most likely scenario. 
 
 
 
Slide #8
 
The third point is the acceptable outcome, or our resistance point, or BATNA. We 
may have to walk away from the negotiation if the outcome is not acceptable. 
 
 
 
Slide #9
 
Our next step is to determine the business positions of each item under different 
scenarios.  
This is also the time to reach out to our internal stakeholders to assess their 
positions.  
The internal negotiation is equally important and challenging as the external 
negotiation.  
The ultimate goal of internal discussion is to formulate our internal stakeholders’ 
positions and interests into the analysis and develop a set of unified positions. 
 
Slide #10
 
For example, our Product Development Department desires to have a broad field of 
use, so that they can develop a product for different industries.  
Our Marketing Department expects to include U.S. and Japan territories in the 
license, and our Accounting Department prefers fixed licensing payment, so that they 
can manage the budgeting and the planning well. 
All of those inputs from different stakeholders are organically weaved into the term-
sheet positions.  
We will revisit the term-sheet positions several times during our negotiation as new 
information comes in.  
So, the term-sheet should be evergreen and tailored to the point when we reach an 
agreement with our counterpart. 
 
Slide #11
 
I needed to emphasize one thing about the term-sheet. The term-sheet should be 
your top secret.  
You should never share your version of the term-sheet with your counterpart.  
You should prepare a shared version of the term-sheet to communicate offers and 
document the negotiation progress with your partners, but do not share your version 
of the term-sheet with your secret information. 
 
Slide #12
 
I suggest you spend a couple of minutes studying the term-sheet, looking into the 
details of those columns.  
The expected outcome, desired outcome, resistant points, and relative importance.  
Study the term-sheets, understand the terms, and the logic behind the three position 
points of each term. 
M3L9b. Systematic Negotiation Process 
 
Slide #1
 
Now, let's talk about engagement discussions and making the business judgment 
aspects of the systematic negotiation process. 
Slide #2
 
One of the primary goals of your engagement discussions with your counterpart, 
particularly in the later stage of negotiation, is to trade on issues or terms.  
We need to prepare a similar term-sheet for our counterpart and collect intelligence 
to estimate their desired outcome, expected results, and resistance positions, their 
badness. 
 
Slide #3
 
Here is some guidance on how to treat issues.  
First, you and your counterpart may value those terms differently.  
Some terms may be more important to them, but less important to you.  
Whenever you identify different interests, follow up and ask questions.  
They may lead to different opportunities.  
Trade issues that are less valuable to you with issues that are more valuable to your 
counterpart. 
Also pay attention to your counterpart's motivation, problems, and business 
limitations.  
If you can offer something to your partner that helps your partner solve their 
problems, you are creating additional value to your counterpart, and you will also 
benefit from that. 
Slide #4
 
There are some overlooked issues. 
Time, risk, and tax and accounting related items.  
Particularly in international negotiations, we need to consider those issues, and they 
may have a significant impact on the value of our agreement. 
 
Slide #5
 
Negotiators frequently make judgment calls during business negotiation. 
Negotiators need to decide how much they should trust the information that their 
counterpart provides. 
What are the impacts of those options on their business and ultimately whether to 
reach an agreement with their counterpart? 
Slide #6
 
It is almost inevitable that negotiators experience those judgment biases that we 
discussed before.  
Some common judgment biases in negotiation are fixed pie assumption, which 
means that both parties enter into a negotiation with an attitude to win. 
Framing bias of negotiator judgment. Present the information in the format of loss or 
gain.  
Irrational escalation of conflict. Overestimating your own value or endowment effect.  
Self serving biases and anchoring biases.  
We will briefly go through how these biases affect the negotiator's intuitive 
reasoning process in the next lectures. 
 
Slide #7
 
If you behave constructively and collaboratively, it is very likely that your 
collaborative approach will lead to some new unexpected opportunities.  
For example, in one license negotiation, we realized that the licensor was seeking 
new opportunities to further develop the technology as its federal sponsored 
research program was in its final years. 
On the other hand, the company, the licensor, would need its group's deep expertise 
in this area to help the company to optimize some designs. Both licensee and 
licensor will benefit from a joint research and development program. So the licensor 
and licensee added the joint research and development program to the negotiation 
term-sheet. 
This is just one of many great examples that when both parties enter a negotiation 
with a win-win attitude and spend enough time to exchange information, try hard to 
identify new opportunities. they can find those opportunities. 
Slide #8
 
Eventually, we reached an agreement.  
The systematic approach, which combined analytical assessment and intuitive 
reasoning, created more value to both parties. 
Also, the term-sheet provided clarity to both organizations. The term-sheet is an 
informative tool that both negotiators can use to communicate their progress and 
outcomes with their internal stakeholders and set the right expectations at both 
sides. 
 
 
Slide #9
 
This table shows the agreement that we reached.

 James Stietenroth
It has been a fairly common practice on the projects I have worked on to have significant scope creep. 
Often, the project manager for the client does not want to go back to their management requesting more
money multiple times.  There are usually some areas that do not use all of the hours they were allotted at
the beginning of the project and those hours become "available" for the project to use.  The custom when
there is additional work that was not in the approved scope has been to track the additional hours spent
doing the work and near the end of a project, when hours are getting short, to develop an estimate to
complete the project and if there is additional funding required then the client's project manager will only
need to request more funding once and the needs are well documented.  I have heard that some of our
competitors will request a change order for nearly anything that was not in the approved scope.  If there
were hours that were not used to complete the work it is customary for them to still charge the project
until there allotted hours are used. 
Recently, we were waiting to hear back about a proposal for a total plant DCS migration which will be
about eight years of work.  I was at a FAT (factory acceptance test) with the client for a much smaller job. 
The client's new automation manager came to witness the FAT.  We started talking about my company's
experience with DCS migrations and we discussed that the refinery was not well documented and not well
maintained.  He stated that the management was very tight with funding.  I explained how we try to work
with the client to get the most work from us without having to request more money.  He said he hadn't
heard of an ENC that would do this before (ENCs sell engineering manhours).  I tried to set up a meeting
between him and my manager to discuss the topic but before the meeting was finalized the client let us
know that we were awarded the work.  Tomorrow I am hosting the client on a tour of our facilities and
leading a meeting between the client management and my management.

in place before arriving at the dealership. I also like having my spouse with me so I can watch the
salesperson try to appeal to my wife's senses and add more accessories or even try to persuade us into
buying a higher level vehicle. My wife is more frugal than I am, so it's not usually a winning strategy. I also
usually have a couple of preliminary quotes in place before I go to a dealership, that way I can discuss
those prices and/or associated options with my wife in front of the salesperson (or at least within earshot)
of them. I make it known upon my arrival at a dealership that I have a pre-approval in place and that I
don't want or need to talk with the Finance Manager to "see if they can get me a better interest rate."
Usually once they hear that we have another viable or even better option than the one they are presenting,
they come back with "their best deal" which I in turn ask for in writing so that I can call my bank. I also
usually ask for a couple of hours to get back with them. That's when the deal is done. I will give a call back
to the original dealership that I originally spoke with to see if they can beat the most recent deal of their
competitor, if they can, they win, if not, I buy from the other dealership.

In watching the lecture on distributive negotiations it made me think of my time as a car salesman.  This
negotiation process was used all the time I just never knew the term.  While I understand ZOPA in its
basic form, it made me think how that can be manipulated by the seller. During pricing negotiations,
obviously the price is involved but a key part in negotiations are payments.  So if the focus is placed on
payments, the ZOPA now becomes how much are you willing to spend per month as opposed how much
do you want to spend for the vehicle.  Now, terms, APR, even your trade etc. come into play which can be
adjusted first before the overall price of the vehicle.  This is why you will have  a car salesman come with a
really high payment with their first offer and always ask you "how much did you want your payments to
be"?  So my word of advice if going to buy a vehicle, already come with a pre approval from your bank and
just have them negotiate on the price.  
It makes me think how in my line of work during any negotiations, if we are not even on the same ZOPA,
so to speak, negotiations could be stalled completely because the focus from each party could be
different.

From my past experience as a Patent Examiner with the USPTO, I know that Intellectual Property or IP is
critically important for a firm's growth and well being.   Some companies are bought and sold based on
their Patent Portfolio.   I was at the Patent Office when the then largest patent infringement case was
settled between Blackberry (RIM) and Campana NTP in the US Supreme Court to the tune of $600
Million.   More on the case can be found here if interested.  https://spectrum.ieee.org/consumer-
electronics/gadgets/the-story-behind-the-blackberry-case
The over riding issue is how to protect intellectual property without jeopardizing loss of control.   IBM has
for years been the company with most approved patents per year at +or- 3000.   To comply with being first
to identify anything new and unique and meet the requirements of USPTO 102(e) the publication date is
(Post is Read)
the deciding
point.  https://www.uspto.gov/sites/default/files/web/offices/dcom/olia/aipa/102eflowchart.pdf
A Patent Examiner's function is to research all Prior Art (which includes publications and myriad data
bases) to ascertain if an idea is unique and first with claiming what ever is being patented.  
Some companies do not publish publicly for this reason and do not file for a patent in order to protect the
loss of their idea.  Kind of a unique conundrum between receiving a patent (that can take years) and just
using the idea without publicly describing or divulging.  Current law protects an issued patent for 20 years
but during that time there are maintenance fees to keep it protected.   During the last recession, many
patents went abandoned as companies either went bankrupt or decided that any particular patent was not
worth the cost of maintaining.  
Mason, what you describe is exactly what I am trying to elucidate.   There is no perfect solution between
sharing information and potentially losing control of your intellectual property.

Research In Motion Ltd., the maker of the BlackBerry e-mail device, Friday announced it has settled

My most recent experience about negotiating a win-win deal took place earlier this summer. I was on
vacation in the Caribbean when I received a text message from my local boss in San Antonio. It turns out
that another employee of our company had recently taken over a Program Manager role in Colorado where
his predecessor from a different company had left him high and dry when it came to turning over some
important network security documentation. The PM is tasked with supporting an important defense
system that my company is ultimately responsible for. My boss apologized for interrupting me during my
vacation, but asked if I would be willing to go to on a short notice trip to Colorado to help our colleague get
things in order there upon my return to the states a few days from then. I asked some preliminary
questions as to not take on a losing situation myself, and I agreed to the trip. Upon finding out that I would
be traveling to Colorado to help our colleague, my division head at our corporate office in Virginia called
me and told me that he was happy that I would be going to help the PM and that he would also be flying
out the same time to have meetings with our customers. To make a long story short, I was able to fly out to
Colorado (great weather in August), assist my corporate colleague (who was very happy), get a couple of
extra paid days off (made me very happy), and get some nice recognition that should go towards a few
more coins and strips of printed paper (which also makes me happy). It was definitely a win-win deal.

Gray,
       Good point. It is important to remain somewhat flexible going into negotiations, because certain topics
or features that one may think is non-negotiable could actually be on the table once the meeting begins. In
most situations, a company or entity (or their representative) goes into meetings with the intent of
achieving an objective and/or garnering a competitive advantage in business through the acquisition of a
product, services, land, or resources. If the proper amount of due diligence does not take place prior to
negotiations, it is likely that the business objective will go unfulfilled and the opportunity to achieve the
aforementioned competitive advantage will be lost. Having a BATNA is thoroughly important, and having
multiple options is almost always a best case scenario.

Our industry has lots of silos concerning product development. This is because we co-develop products

We are also in the difficult position in that some of our customers also try to make a competing product.

customer.
Definitely a case of having to work together but controlling the information.

You definitely hit on an important part work offer negotiations.   In past lives, I did a fair amount of salary
reviews and motivational assessments.  Turns out money although important is not always the top
concern.  The willing and readiness to get out of bed and show up is by far a high note on everyone's list of
motivators.  
During my tenure in the US Air Force, a world wide survey was done to try and ascertain what some of the
issues were and what could be done to not only improve readiness but also increase retention and
especially in critical need skills where training was expensive.   
You might be surprised to learn that pay was on the list but no where near the top of said list even though
we were not particularly high paid "employees". 
High on the list of grievances were poor food, poor billets (barracks), lost or delayed mail and pay
problems that included incorrect amounts or mis-directed pay checks (we did not quite have direct deposit
then) especially when stationed overseas.  
I encountered both frustrations.   The military pay system was centralized and automated using an IBM
(Post is Read)
system with the green treasury check punch cards like IRS tax refund checks used to have. 
https://www.dfas.mil/
  This meant that all pertinent information was input via a keypunch operator.  This included things like
name and service number as well as amounts.  Just before my four year anniversary of service, I was
promoted (yeah more $) and stationed in Madrid, Spain.   Lo and behold when my first newly minted and
higher paycheck was supposed to arrive, there was nothing in my base post office box.   I was not living pay
check to pay check by then so waited.  After the second pay period with no check arrived, I went to the base
pay office that then they had to contact the pay center in Denver (new consolidated location mentioned
above and noted in the URL).   Took a few days but turns out my name had been changed from Lyons to
Lynch so the postal clerk (an Airman like me) did not put the checks in my mail box.   Fortunately, the
checks were still on base and not sent back to Denver.   
After convincing said clerk to give me the checks all I had to do was attempt to cash them.   With a written
letter of authorization from the Squadron Commander, I was instructed to sign the checks with my new
name and below with my true name.  Took several pay cycles for this keypunch mistake to be vetted out
and corrected.
My second more humorous experience was a letter I received about one and a half years from when it was
received at the same Madrid Air Force mail room . This was after I was off Active Duty and living in Austin,
TX attending school at tu.   Turns out the letter must have fallen on the floor as it arrived in a plastic bag
and  in tact but with foot prints on both sides.   
Needless to say both pay and mail were high on the list of Air Force personnel complaints.  
Hope that you get a chuckle or two from this story. 
John Lyons aka John Lynch.

My most recent win-win negotiation was selling my home and buying a new house. The market here in
DFW is great for sellers, but brutal for buyers at the moment.
In selling, I had a multiple offer situation, which was fantastic, but choosing the right offer was more than
just who was willing to pay the most for my home. The home I wanted to buy, the seller's were building
new, so they needed a month long lease back - so I needed a buyer for my home that would be willing to do
the same for me. A lot of the high offers for the home I was selling, wanted to close immediately, so I
couldn't accept them. I also had several people that offered a little above asking price, but then they agreed
to pay some of the items that seller's would traditionally pay - so technically their offer was even more
above asking. In the end, it was one of these offers that I picked, and the buyer was renting close by so he
had the flexibility to allow me to stay until the seller's of my new home moved out.
In purchasing, I had to make my offer stand out as homes are getting multiple offers quite regularly. So to
do that, I did the same as some of the offers I received. I offered to pay some of the things that a seller
would traditionally pay, and I was willing to go along with the 30 day lease back. I also noticed when
viewing the home, the sellers were animal lovers. (Trophies were displayed from winning various
equestrian events, and pictures of their dog were in several places in the home.) So I wrote a letter to the
seller, appealing to the common thread we both had as animal lovers. Not sure if the letter helped me or
not, but I got the house - so I like to think that the letter was what won them over. :)
Of course I did not know all of the fancy terms, like BATNA and ZOPA, when in this situation - but it does
prove that finding common values and interests in a negotiation is key. If both sides feel they are getting
some value, then everyone walks away happy.

The underlying academic principle of winner's curse is the prospect theory that we discussed in the first
module. The utility and value curve has two sessions one is above the horizontal axis, which describes 'risk
aversion' behavior when people look at gains. The other is below horizontal axis, which explains 'risk
taking' behaviors when people experience loss. Human beings tend to be over optimistic about the chance
of "win back" when look at loss. The pain of losing one hundred is greater than the happiness from gaining
$100. However, the incremental pain of losing additional $100 is less than losing the first $100. This
psychological behavior explains why gamblers want to bid more after they lose. Bidding is also similar,
after losing one round to a competing bidder, one's attitude toward the value can dramatically change.

I think whenever you deal with relationships you are constantly negotiating win-win situations. This can
include a wife, a girlfriend, siblings etc. However, some negotiations can sneak up on you. (literally)
One time I was getting a lease signed by a farmer located on a rural property. After driving down a dirt
road for 5 min and then across a driveway that was nothing more than a path that his truck made from
the road to his house, from years of taking the same route every day over the years, I came upon a small
house. I parked at what I considered a reasonable distance from the front,  grabbed my leather
satchel and headed to the door. I did not see his vehicle parked anywhere, so I figured I would just leave the lease and a nice note
which I had prepared in advance for such an occasion. After, placing the 
note on the door, I turned to make the trek back to my car. As I turned the corner of the house to get to my car, I was met by two
very large and very surprised dogs (apparently they were napping in the
barn). Now, I really like dogs and I am very familiar with dogs and their behavior. These dogs were not friendly and the alpha was
looking for a sign of weakness. It was a very tense situation. There was no
way to make it to the car in time. It was at least 10 secs at a full sprint and 45 sec walk. In either case, I was looking at a very
undesirable outcome. So, I decided to negotiate.
Fortunately, I had not eaten lunch and it was in my bag. I decided to start the negotiations by slowly reaching in and pulling out two
turkey sandwiches. They were moving closer,  and still had an aggressive
stance, stiff and ridged, especially the hind legs, tail raised, fur still standing up and their ears flat against their heads, However,
upon seeing the sandwiches they had stopped growling. Once, I removed the
sandwiches from the baggies they relaxed a bit and their ears came up. That is when I knew I created some value and it was no
longer a zero-sum negotiation. I tossed each dog a sandwich, the alpha first.
It doesn't take long for a large dog to eat a sandwich and I needed at least 45 secs. So, while they were discussing the terms (aka
eating the sandwiches) I opened my bag of Cheetos. Now, I needed 45

seconds, and I was hoping they needed the delicious cheesy goodness that is located in a big bag of Cheetos. Turns out this was an

exchange of my lunch for 45 seconds of time, and they seemed to be happy with my lunch in exchange for that time. All said and
done, I think it was a win-win negotiation. 
Remember when going to a stranger's house always check for dog bowls before you get out of the car.  :)

We've adopted the win-win strategy quite a bit here at work. Our owners have recently asked us to make
budget cuts, almost beyond reasonable when it comes to equipment maintenance. In order to continue
operating an aging fleet by repairing the major items, we have taken to negotiation with companies for
(Post is Read)
parts, and or components.
The first few attempts at this were somewhat chaotic, but have since found systems that work. Typically we
can approach a vendor who has components for equipment that are either out of service, or not being
utilized as frequently anymore. After we perform some research to see what they have in inventory, we
offer trades or swaps on items we have of value. We have traded road maintainers for engines that can be
rebuilt, or components, and anything that can be negotiated ethically and within the business parameters.
Occasionally we negotiate win-win deals by paying well in advance for items, or securing work in the future
(backlog) with a company for a significant repair to obtain a discount.
I use similar tactics for technology as well. If we have outdated technology, we will barter for upgrades, or
guarantees of purchases and service contracts to attempt to decrease the amount spent for that year. My
takeaway from these approaches has been to build a relationship with the other party and understand what
they want to accomplish in the future. Sometimes it's agreements, other times it's purchases, or simply an
opportunity to be able to bid for a portion of work (not bid rigging, but rather the opportunity)

 Andrew Burgess
Hello All,
My experience about a win - win deal goes back to 2012 when I was working at a very small company
(annual turnover approx $800,000).
We were developing a new technology at the time and looking for a test site to trial it out.
During this time, we received an enquiry from a Chevron facility in Kazakhstan who were looking at the
established offering our company had. We proposed trialling this new solution out to the guys at site then
the next day, I received a phone call from one of the TA's at Chevron in California who had caught wind of
this discussion. He wished to fly out to our (very small) HQ for a meeting to discuss this technology in
great detail within the next few days.
To our surprise,we were very grateful for the interest at the time and when he arrived he couldn't have
been a more humble down - to earth individual. He explained to us that as early adopters of new
technology, Chevron would like to trial this technique at site for proof of concept before committing to any
purchase of hardware.
We agreed to do this and sent an engineer (our best) to accompany the TA to site in Kazakhstan to conduct
a 5 - day pilot project. Thankfully,this was a resounding success and not only did we have a successful
proof of concept, the data we collected allowed us to refine the solution further and streamline the offering.
Sensing a big opportunity to gain market penetration, we then appealed to the TA's academic ego and
suggested that we should co-author a joint paper at the PCIC conference the coming year. This was a win
for us as it gave us a huge partner to vouch for and effectively rubber stamp our technology amongst a large
target market. It was also win for him as he was first to the post among his peers in identifying and
implementing this new technology. 
I have attached a copy of the paper for anyone who is interested (I am pleased to report this work was
awarded best paper at the conference during that year) and we were subsequently awarded over
$6,000,000's worth of work from this single Chevron site over the next 4 years.
This exercise taught me how to appeal to different people's natures and identify what they are looking for
in a negotiation. It also taught me to reach common ground as quickly as possible to expedite a negotiation
process and advance swiftly to a position both parties are happy with. 
Thanks for reading!
BR,
Andrew

 Taylor Leach
In my relatively new position on a product support team, I deal with a variety of
individuals every day.  Some folks are good about the different routes we can take
to solve a problem.  Others - let's just say not so much.
For example, if they are having an issue with software on their machine and I
know the don't really care to start a remote session where I can see their screen, I
frame the situation and give them different scenarios.  I start off by offering we
contact the end user's IT group and I can conference them in while we discuss
what happens and they make the changes to the software.  The other option is I
remote in real quick, make some minor and most likely quick changes, and the
issue can be fixed!
If you see what I did there, you'll notice I made the option of me fixing the
problem a lot more enticing.  The reason I frame it this way is because most of the
time, the end user's IT group is a third party or out-sourced IT company.  Most of
the people I work with prefer to not get those IT groups involved because it would
take literally a full week to get someone available to help get this issue fixed.  So
for time and money's sake, the customer usually becomes a lot more comfortable
with me taking care of the issue even though they usually wouldn't be okay with
sharing their screen with me.  In the end, I believe this to also be a win-win
scenario.  Customer gets his issue resolved and is more comfortable talking to my
team and I get a positive survey from the customer.

I'm chagrined to consider my recent track record regarding win-win negotiation
because I can see that I've slipped into a zero-sum bias. I can see it most clearly in
the way I've behaved with my colleagues, as Buck described. We're growing,
expanding beyond our startup team, and I think I've allowed fear to color my
behavior. Fear that I'll lose status or influence. Fear that there won't be enough
pie! Not at all attractive or productive.
Luckily I've also experienced the benefit of win-win negotiations. I used to do
program development and grant writing for a large social services organization in
Central New York. State and local funding for programs was very scarce, and we
were in constant competition with other agencies who were also doing great work
in the same city. I started watching Federal RFPs more closely and noticed that
(Post is Unread)
there were some that me might be competitive for - but only if we worked
together. Our CEO agreed to let me spend to time researching and writing, and he
made some introductions to two other "competing" oranizations. We came up
with a plan for dividing the proposed service delivery (dental, behavioral, general
practice, etc.). Everyone contributed time to planning, and each organization
pledged a level of "matching" support. We wouldn't each get an equal share of the
grant funding, but everyone would have the opportunity to extend their reach and
impact. And we secured a federal grant to continue the work!

In someone else’s post I addressed the issue of being able to trust the person you
are negotiating with.  In my line of work the typical way I negotiate with people is
on a bid price for a construction project.  Sometimes this is a large project and
other times it is just a day rate but either way there is often times some form of
negotiation. 
I am honestly not a big fan of negotiation but I know it is part of business and you
must work on it and be successful in it if you want to be accomplished in your
work.  One of the reasons I am not a fan of negotiating is because typically the
price I give to complete a project is what it is going to cost me to do the project
and there really is no wiggle room in the price.  I am not a fan of adding a percent
on top of my final price to allow for negotiating room but with some companies I
know they are going to want to negotiate on the price, after I figure that out, any
price I give those companies I add a percent to my bid price to give them room to
negotiate.  In my opinion the time spent negotiating is a waste of time when the
price offered is a good price because if they would just accept my price then they
could already have the contract completed and work could start, which would
mean the project would be completed sooner and they could already be seeing a
ROI.  That being said, I understand why many companies want to negotiate a
price because if they did not attempt to get a lower price then they would not be
doing their job. 
The issue I have with the above statements about negotiating bid price is that
typically I am working with a project manager with a client company that should
have some idea of the cost to complete the project but many times they do not
and the only way they can estimate a price on the project is based off of all of the
bids or an initial estimate gave to them from an outside source.  It should not be
this way, these project managers should be able to make an estimate on the
project and then negotiate on the price they have come up with, not bid shopping
and trying to get me to lower my price based off of someone else’s estimate or
simply trying to get me to lower my price just on principle because they think any
price given to them should be lowered. 
Due to all of the above reason’s I typically like working on large project with
project managers with our client companies I know, because this way I know
when they want to negotiate the price it is because it is necessary and not just
(Post is Unread)
because they want to try and make a little extra money.  I have no problem with
someone wanting to make a little extra profit or reduce their cost but when it is
unreasonable then I take issue with it.
I prefer the to offer the best price I can to reduce negotiating time and when
people doubt me on that based off of inaccurate information (prices from
companies that are incompetent/companies that continually loose money or are
trying to push competition out but bidding extremely low and then trying to
make it up on change orders), it frustrates me.  If they are negotiating based off of
good data and accurate information then I completely understand.

I want to share a few separate win-win scenarios because I am trying to
incorporate what we are learning not only in my professional life but a bit into my
personal life as well.
My first example has to do with me getting involved with another sport.  I have
never been an outstanding athlete, but I am pretty decent and would like to think
that I hold my own.  I am also VERY competitive.  As a long distance runner
dating all the way back to junior high, endurance and I have always been very
close friends.  One sport I never got involved with due to small town culture is
soccer.  I've played most other sports and knew the general concepts of soccer, but
it never caught my eye until this year.  I have a co-worker who is a HUGE soccer
fan.  Some of his passion for the game has rubbed off on me I suppose and we
occasionally put a soccer game on in the office on a TV we have on the wall.
Well, he was telling me one day that he has a bunch of people that play in a "pick-
up" game of soccer just to run around for a few hours as a way to stay in shape and
play the game they all love so much.  The only problem is usually the team is one
player short for the field they play on.  So I started thinking about playing and
mentioned it to him.  I let him know up front that I had never played soccer before
which he knew already.  
In the end, I've been playing for about 3 months now with my new team and have
learned quite a bit more about soccer than I have already known which is mostly
just knowledge learned from ESPN.  Our team and my colleague win because they
now have a "full" team for the field they play on, and I win because I get to play
(Post is Read)
and learn another sport and join a new team in my area.
My second example involves a defect in a product that I support.  We have a
product that I have become very fond because it involves a lot of IT knowledge. 
This product virtualizes a lot of our hardware so that programming and planning
of a project can be done in advance and in an office instead of on a customer's
site.  One of our larger partners found a huge issue with the product that
virtualizes hardware.  It turns out that when you try to modify the project within
the virtualized environment, the project would then become corrupt causing the
customer to lose all their work.  This impacted business performance and was a
huge issue if someone spent several weeks creating an environment to be
deployed on a customer's site.
Well, I ended up working with this partner over the next few weeks.  I ended up
taking a backup of their server and their environment and recreating it in my own
virtual environment.  After quite some time, I finally recovered the partner's work
and found a work-around until R&D fixed the issue in a new software release. 
Since I was able to recover the work, he was able to deploy the project and make a
customer happy which resulted in everyone being successful.
Now, we still had the issue with the virtualization product.  Our partner raised
quite a bit of hell because they knew that this was going to happen again and did
not have the leeway to delay projects for a week and a half like we did previously. 
After speaking with my manager, I talked to partner and asked if I could train him
and a few of his colleagues in the work-around that I found until R&D fixed the
issue.  While he was reluctant at first, I convinced him that this was the best way
to move forward so that no one loses money or time and the customer's remain
happy with timelines and the solutions.
After training this partner and his team, the partner agreed that this was the best
way forward until a new version of the product was released and was happy with
the work-around.  He won because his company could continue forward with
projects.  I won because a partner and customer were happy, and we did not lose
that business to the competition. 
I actually consider this a win-win-win because R&D found two additional issues to
fix on top of the one I sent to them.  They were able to fix all three issues and
release a new version of the product before any other customers found the original
flaw in the older release.

Howdy Folks! As my travels to Europe wind down (for this year at least) I
continue to be amazed how different styles of negotiation take place and the
different gestures, facial expressions, attitudes, etc. that different cultures express.
In Asia, for example, trust is of the utmost importance and quite frankly, the
deciding factor in most cases. In Europe, you can have scenarios to which trust is
important, however quality/price are the main drivers. 
(Post is Read)
Quick story; we were in the final negotiation phase of hiring an insulation
company to insulate our piping and tanks. The European sales manager
mentioned that we could get a much better price if they sourced the material from
their Asian office; however the quality was not very good. Understanding that our
facility is on the North Sea and the winters here are brutal, quality isn't something
we were interested in sacrificing. Their competitor, a Dutch based company
mentioned that we could source the material from Europe and have their local
folks do the install. The other company had to fly in people from Poland. (Not that
far away from The Netherlands, nonetheless the deciding factor; cost wise). We
ended up with the Dutch company, even though they were a bit more expensive
for the following reasons:
-Local contacts
-Spoke the local language to communicate with our main contractor
-Understood the regulations/laws of The Netherlands
Point: Having a local presence and understanding of the culture/laws/language,
in my opinion, is worth paying a bit more for!
Any thoughts?
Pablo

the new plant.  I wrote these instructions over a year ago before we opened up the plant with the

scenarios that the new plant could encounter but I was mindful that the
documents would have to be edited later to "fit" the new plant. In February of this
year, I trained the personell on how to make product, maintain product
traceability, etc per the written instructions. The ISO audit in Russia was
scheduled for this past week. The win win story follows:
Since February, I have revised the documents multiple times to be able to adapt to
the different scenarios that they have encountered during the roll up of
production. These have involved extensive negotiations via email, phone and text
with the plant manager in Russia as well as the Quality liaison in that hemisphere.
Being fresh and new at building our product, the plant manager had several ideas
on how to make the product that deviated from the written instructions. I was
under strict instructions from Houston management not to deviate from the
process made here. The plant manager had several excellent ideas that lent more
to their style of production which is high volume/low variety. In Houston we are
high variety/low volume. These two methodologies require different process steps
as long as you don't sacrifice quality. I incorporated the ideas from the plant
manager and wrote them into the work instruction. I calculated the cycle times
Houston vs Russia and I then took this data to Houston management. I was able
to negotiate the changes successfully and Russia got what they wanted. At the end
of the day, they were included in the decision making of their plant and it is
starting to feel that they are finally engaging and standing on their own while
making their own decisions. 
Long story short, I just found out today that they passed their ISO audit and are
now ISO certified. I could not be more proud of those guys. We have come a long
way in less than a year!

 Joshua Barnard
Seller was in her 90's
Seller was not buying another home after this
Seller had kids in their 60's which were acting as a voice of reason
Roof was at least 20 years old
Still some large pieces of furniture left in the home as well as appliances
Home had a dated interior design despite being built in the 1990's
No foundation problems like every single home within this price range I had seen
One of my more recent negotiation dealings has been buying a home back at the
end of 2016. I would call it a win-win situation because at the time my realtor was
feeding me the old "it's a hot market" language and said it would behoove me to
get the seller on contract quickly so the home didn't get snatched from under us or
so we didn't get pulled into a bidding war. So, we offered them exactly what they
were asking, which I wasn't a fan of, however it was then time to collect more in
depth data on the home and seller. What I gathered was:
After finding out about the roof I was determined to either get a new roof out of
this deal or walk away. Doing some research I found that insurance premiums
were going to be unreasonably high for such an old roof, and you need insurance if
you're going to finance. After learning a little about the seller I proposed the idea
that she make an insurance claim, thus getting a roof for me and there wouldn't be
any ramifications for her since she wouldn't be a home owner any longer. At the
same time I used this as an opportunity to install proper attic ventilation free of
cost since now was the time to do it. Additionally, I told my realtor, and I don't
know if it ever made it's way to the seller, that if they didn't accommodate the new
roof then I would not be able to go any further into this process. Furthermore, no
one who had to finance would be able to either since the insurance rates were so
unreasonably high. That gave them only one option which was to settle for a lesser
offer from a cash buyer, typically an investor. I said they should view it as an
investment into the home that required minimum cost, since if I were to walk
away from the deal, at least now they can advertise it as having a new roof to draw
in more buyers.
At first the seller was reluctant to agree however the more rational children of hers
saw my viewpoint and were able to reach through to her. Later on I had caught
wind that the seller was trying to make arrangements to sell and/or move the
appliances and furniture still in the home. This was another cost that I would have
to incur since I had minimal furniture and no appliances. I offered for them to
(Post is Read)
keep anything they wanted in the home and I would bring what I didn't want to
the dump or donate it so it would save them the trouble. I also saw the dining
room set; table, chairs, hutch, and asked to have that as part of the contract with
the home. They agreed but it caused some delays due to getting signatures which I
suppose had them worried that I would walk away this late in the game (we had
already pushed the closing date out twice). To alleviate their worries they had
asked that I move the utilities into my name, set for the original closing date,
which would have been only a few days prior to the new closing date. Whether this
was for nefarious reasons (I found a water leak a month later) or not, I'm not sure
and I don't see how that would have changed anything, but at the time it seemed
silly. Utilities for a week would have cost less than $50 so I would mark that down
as a "do not care" item in my Term Sheet, and I used this issue in trade for
something that the seller did care about.
All in all I felt successful. What started as a not so wise bid, and knowing the
future water leak, would have pushed me into Winners Curse territory, I was able
to get a new roof, attic vents, gutters, perfectly good refrigerator, stove, washer,
dryer, dining room table, chairs, and a large hutch which I would probably value
at ~$5000-10,000 plus no effort on my part having to organize all of it. The seller
got to quickly sell the home, no added costs to her, didn't have to move some
extremely large and fragile items that remained after they had done an estate sale
of sorts, and didn't have to find a place to store it since she wasn't going into
another home...
